subject: Accounting
title: Source Documents
description: A quick, practical guide to Source Documents.

hook.text: No receipt, no entry. Every bookkeeping record needs a source document to prove it happened.

buildup.text: Invoices, receipts, bank statements, contracts—these are the evidence behind every transaction.

discovery.text: Source documents provide date, amount, parties involved, and the nature of the transaction.

twist.text: Lost documents can make audits impossible and tax deductions unclaimable. Filing matters.

climax.text: Digital bookkeeping has replaced shoeboxes of receipts—but the principle remains: document everything.

punchline.text: If you can't prove it happened, it didn't happen.

quiz.question: Why are source documents important in bookkeeping?
options: They prove that transactions actually occurred
They replace the need for accounting

details.summary: Source documents are the original records—invoices, receipts, contracts, and bank statements—that provide evidence of financial transactions. This topic explains which documents to keep, how long to retain them, and their role in maintaining an audit trail.
details.whyItMatters: Without source documents, bookkeeping entries lack proof. They are the first line of defense in audits, tax disputes, and legal proceedings requiring verification of financial activity.
takeaways: Every journal entry should be traceable back to a source document as evidence
Common source documents include invoices, receipts, bank statements, and contracts
Most tax authorities require businesses to retain source documents for at least seven years

faq.question: What are source documents in bookkeeping?
faq.answer: Source documents are the original records that prove a financial transaction occurred—invoices from suppliers, sales receipts, bank statements, contracts, payroll records, and purchase orders. They provide the evidence trail behind every entry in the books.

faq.question: How long should businesses keep source documents?
faq.answer: The IRS recommends keeping most records for at least three years, but seven years is safer for many document types. Records related to employment taxes should be kept for four years. Some documents like corporate records should be kept permanently.
